Specifically, standard self-report instruments require participants to translate their inner states into verbal language, a process that introduces systematic error whenever the experience is difficult to articulate (Çalışkan & Kapucu, 2023; Davidson & Kaszniak, 2015; Grossman, 2019; Varela & Shear, 1999). Despite growing interest in meditation research and its psychological and health-related benefits (Baminiwatta & Solangaarachchi, 2021; Goldberg et al., 2022), this measurement gap has remained largely unaddressed (Sieder et al., 2024; Van Dam et al., 2018).

Meditation outcomes have primarily been investigated using self-report questionnaires (Gherardi-Donato et al., 2020; Karl & Fischer, 2022), neuroimaging techniques (Treves et al., 2024), and behavioral tasks (Hadash & Bernstein, 2019). However, these approaches face several limitations. Existing questionnaires often show inconsistent psychometric properties across studies, including unstable latent structures, variable item content, and limited cross-cultural validity (Choi et al., 2021; Christopher et al., 2014; Karl et al., 2020; Lecuona et al., 2024; Muris & Otgaar, 2020). Moreover, given that self-report methods rely on participants' ability to introspect and verbally describe their experiences, several factors may affect the response process in meditation assessments, such as: meditation experience (e.g., Alvear et al., 2022; Choi et al., 2021); educational background (He et al., 2024); or cultural and linguistic differences (e.g., Feng et al., 2017; Karl et al., 2020). Taken together, these factors highlight the risk of various biases in meditation measurements, potentially undermining the instruments' reliability and validity.

Although tools have been developed to assess meditative experiences while addressing these factors, existing frameworks still fail to capture the complexity and multidimensionality of these states fully (Lutz et al., 2015; Timmermann et al., 2023). Indeed, meditative states are complex because they vary along several partly independent dimensions (e.g., attentional stability, meta-awareness, affective tone, bodily experience, and the sense of self) that need not co-vary, so that no single score or latent factor can summarize them without loss of information (Lindahl et al., 2017; Lutz et al., 2015). To overcome these limitations, idiographic approaches such as micro-phenomenology (i.e., use of guided retrospective interviews to elicit and analyse fine-grained descriptions of specific meditative experiences revealing their moment-to-moment unfolding and initially unnoticed aspects), have been proposed by facilitating access to lived experience (Lutz et al., 2024; Petitmengin, 2006; Petitmengin et al., 2019; Ritunnano et al., 2023). While promising, these methods often involve small sample sizes, require extensive training, and rely on participants' ability to verbalize experiences. Therefore, there remains a need for complementary tools that facilitate introspective access without relying on verbal report and linguistic introspection (Davidson & Kaszniak, 2015; Lindahl et al., 2017; Varela & Shear, 1999).

Non-verbal pictographic tools may offer a complementary way of capturing meditation experiences. Through visual representation rather than verbal description, they may reduce reliance on linguistic introspection and provide a more direct access to experiential content. For instance, the Self-Assessment Manikin (SAM; Bradley & Lang, 1994) was developed to measure different states such as emotional responses and it was shown to be language-free, culture-independent, and faster to complete without sacrificing sensitivity or reliability (Morris, 1995). Similarly, the Inclusion of others in the self (IOS; Aron et al., 1992), measuring interpersonal connectedness, and the Pictorial Representation of Illness and Self Measure (PRISM; Sensky & Büchi, 2016), show good psychometric properties in groups for whom standard questionnaires pose comprehension difficulties (Brady et al., 2019; Büchi et al., 2002).

In meditation, however, pictographic measurement remains substantially underdeveloped. To the best of the authors' knowledge, few pictographic tools have been developed. These include the Perceived Body Boundaries Scale (PBBS; Dambrun, 2016), which measures the degree to which one experiences the self as a distinct, separate entity from the surrounding; the Spatial Frame of Reference Continuum (SFoRC, Hanley & Garland, 2019), which is designed to assess the extent to which individuals perceive their sense of self as extending beyond their physical bodies; and the Inclusion of Nature in Self scale (INS; Schultz, 2001) and the Extended Inclusion of Nature in Self scale (EINS; Martin & Czellar, 2016), which measure connectedness with nature. Despite their potential, these instruments each capture a single dimension of meditative experiences and do not completely represent the full range of meditative phenomena.

A further methodological consideration concerns the structural assumptions of conventional psychometric models. Traditional reflective latent-variable approaches treat items as interchangeable indicators of an underlying construct (Borsboom et al., 2021), which conflicts with the phenomenological diversity of meditation experiences. That is, each experience is not interchangeable but unique in its own right, and their diversity is a feature of the construct, warning against reduction by latent variables. Although reflective models can still be applied if each meditation state is considered a latent construct, literature has reported item inflation and highly complex factor structures due to their diversity (Gamma & Metzinger, 2021). This makes reflective models inefficient, creating a challenge in psychometric measurement. Instead, single-item measures may pose a more efficient and realistic way to map these highly complex, embodied and experiential phenomena.

Single-item measures require confronting two problems at once. The first is that transfer of psychometric properties from multi-item to single-item instruments is difficult or in some aspects impossible (e.g., internal consistency is undefined, or factor structures and relations with other constructs cannot be recovered; Allen et al., 2022). The second is that validity evidence must come from several sources, and often heterogeneous and insufficient combinations of sources are reported (Flake & Fried, 2020). We therefore organize the present study around established frameworks of validity as a multiple-source unified argument (AERA, APA, & NCME, 2014). More concretely, we propose that single-item development and validation requires evidence on contents, response processes, sensitivity to change, relation with other variables, predictive capability, and internal structure (e.g., Matthews et al., 2022). In addition, we extend it to reliability sources designed for single-item measurement (e.g., Wanous & Hudy, 2001). Rather than a series of independent analyses, each source is treated as one side of a coordinated argument, designed to cross-check one another. For example, response-process evidence qualifies structural findings, criterion relations are interpreted in light of reliability, and convergences and divergences among sources themselves become diagnostic of what each item measures. Meditation research is a particularly demanding case for such a framework, since its constructs are often non-verbal, phenomenologically subtle, and psychometrically complex (Grossman, 2019; Lecuona et al., 2020).

Building on this framework, the present study develops and validates the Meditation Pictographic Inventory (MPI), a pictographic, item-level instrument designed to assess distinct meditation-related experiences using pictographic representations. The MPI treats each meditation state as an item-level construct rather than as an indirect reflection of a latent variable, that is, single-item measures. This approach is more efficient because it provides broad experiential coverage of meditation states. Moreover, because no item derives its meaning from a shared latent variable, the MPI is modular: items can be administered independently or in theory-driven subsets. This property makes the MPI suited both to applied users and researchers, and to mapping multidimensional phenomenology of meditation experiences. In addition, MPI pictographic items based on phenomenological evidence are intended to reduce reliance on verbal description in meditation research. The development and validation of the MPI proceeded in two phases. Phase 1 focused on item development and the establishment of content and response-process validity through expert-informed refinement.

Phase 2 examined psychometric evidence in a general population using a randomized controlled design comparing three meditation practices and an active control condition (CG) before and after a brief meditation practice. Importantly, this study does not seek to provide the MPI as a finalized instrument. Given its modular design, it is conceived as an open set of items that can be extracted, tested, and refined independently, and future versions are expected to revise or extend its content. Accordingly, the present study provides initial validity and reliability evidence for each item, together with a framework through which such evidence can be accumulated.

Phase 1 -MPI Development

Item development followed a combined top-down and bottom-up approach. First, we conducted a narrative review of various theoretical and empirical papers on meditation-related experiences, focusing on frameworks aiming to classify phenomenological dimensions (e.g., Dahl et al., 2015; Dambrun, 2021; Gamma & Metzinger, 2021; Lindahl et al., 2017; Lutz et al., 2015; Van Dam et al., 2018; Yaden et al., 2017). For each framework, we compiled the proposed definitions, examples, and associated domains. For example, Dahl et al. (2015) contributed a functional typology (attentional, constructive, and deconstructive practices); Lutz et al. (2015) emphasized cognitive and affective processes such as dereification and absorption; Van Dam et al. (2018) highlighted conceptual ambiguities in operationalizing meditation-related phenomena; Gamma and Metzinger (2021) provided a taxonomy of altered states, including ineffability and time distortion; and Lindahl et al. (2017) systematically documented adverse experiences. Other sources (e.g., Chiesa & Malinowski, 2011; Dambrun, 2021) informed how self-related and contextual factors shape meditative experience. All constructs were then organized into cognitive, affective, perceptual, somatic, self-related, social, and conative domains. This comparative matrix allowed us to identify redundancies, overlaps, and conceptual gaps across frameworks.

Next, each construct was independently evaluated by three authors (YD, MW, AC) in a triangulation-of-opinions procedure, in which constructs were rated as "necessary", "relevant", or "exclude" based on empirical evidence, conceptual clarity, and representability as pictographic items. Those considered necessary and pictographically representable were retained, while the others were excluded. Disagreements were resolved through collaborative discussion until full consensus was achieved. This collaborative process ensured rigorous evaluation of each dimension and its suitability for inclusion in the MPI. Through this process, an initial set of 21 items was selected, including absorption, body awareness, body boundaries, compassion, decentering, distortion of time, emotional Emotional Reactivity, emotional stability, ineffability, mental effort, mind wandering, negative affect, positive affect, reference continuum, self-compassion, self-criticism, self-nature connectedness, self-other connectedness, sense-of-self (ego), time disappearing, and warmth. Although affect-related dimensions (positive and negative affect) were retained because of their recurrent presence across frameworks, they are conceptualized here as contextual or consequential aspects of meditation, rather than as defining characteristics of the practice itself (Van Dam et al., 2024).

Definitions of all constructs are provided in Section S1.1 of the Supplementary Materials.

In collaboration with a graphic designer, an initial pictographic version of the MPI was created. Three of these items were adapted from previous pictographic measures with the authors' permission (IOS, Aron et al., 1992; PBBS, Dambrun, 2016; SFoRC, Hanley & Garland, 2019). A preliminary comprehensibility check was conducted with a convenience sample of more than ten researchers at the authors' institution, none of whom had meditation experience. Participants were shown each pictographic item and asked whether its general meaning was visually accessible. The check resulted in minor graphic design adjustments to improve visual clarity before the items were presented to expert meditators. To ensure content validity, we then conducted interviews with meditation practitioners to verify that each item accurately represented its intended construct.

Method

Sample and procedure

In total, 10 experts participated in the semi-structured interviews. The inclusion criteria were at least 2,000 hours of practice in their lifespan and regular daily practice. The experts were compensated with €50 for their participation. This phase was conducted in January 2024.

The interviews typically lasted 2h. Two interviews were conducted in person, while the remaining eight were held online via Zoom, depending on the experts' availability. Given the exploratory, content-driven nature of the study, we conducted semi-structured interviews combining interviewing probes (Willis, 2005), as previously applied to mindfulness measures (Belzer et al., 2013; Christopher et al., 2014), with open questions adapted from phenomenological interviewing (Petitmengin, 2006), with approximately 10 questions per item.

The interviews had the following objectives: first, to understand whether each pictographic item accurately represents what they are intended to measure. The items were presented to the experts one by one, without specifying what they represented. The interpretation process was guided by questions such as: "Where do you place yourself at this moment on a scale from one to seven?", "How do you know you feel this way?", "Can you explain why you selected this rating (e.g., 5) rather than a slightly lower or higher value (e.g., 4 or 6) on the scale?" , "What made you doubt your response?", "What does this drawing represent to you?". Second, the interviewer presented what the item actually represented according to the researchers' objective, and asked questions about its representational accuracy (e.g., "Do you believe this drawing represents well what it is intended to represent?", "Should it be represented differently?" and if the response is yes, "Could you please explain to me why, and could you please draw it for me?"). Finally, the experts were invited to add missing concepts related to meditative experiences and to share general comments. Example questions were: "Do you think there are some items which are missing, if you do, which one?", "Why do you think it is important to add this item?", "How would you represent it?", "Is there any concept you believe it is better to eliminate?", "Is there anything else you want to add regarding the questionnaires in general?". The interviewer then thanked the expert and closed the interview.

Data analysis

All the interviews were transcribed using Transkriptor (https://transkriptor.com/) and analyzed following Consensual Qualitative Research approach (CQR; Hill, 2015), a rigorous qualitative research method that involves a team-based analysis of textual data, such as interview transcripts. Two co-authors (YD, MW) independently coded each interview into domains (e.g., interpretation of the pictogram, perceived accuracy, suggested modifications, missing constructs) and core ideas, and then met to reach consensus. A third co-author (AC) acted as auditor, reviewing the consensus versions and resolving remaining disagreements. The research team collaboratively reached a consensus on the findings at each stage of the data analysis while actively working to identify and set aside potential biases. Recognizing that meditation practices yield varied experiences and expert interpretations, we considered each expert's background when analyzing responses. This process supported content validity by examining whether each pictogram accurately represented the intended concept. Finally, the audited results were used to revise the items, and the revised MPI was returned to the designer for final implementation.

Results and Discussion

The sample consisted of experts affiliated with both Buddhist (n = 5) and secular (n = 5) approaches, with an average practice duration of 17.8 years (SD = 11.06, range = 6-35 years). The time spent practicing varied among participants, with some practicing 6-7 hours per week (n = 3), 1-2 hours per day (n = 3), or 10-30 minutes per day (n = 4). Regarding continuity of practice, four participants reported no interruptions, while six experienced interruptions ranging from 1 month to 7 years. The experts engaged in a variety of meditation practices, including Insight (vipassana, open monitoring), loving-kindness (Metta) or compassion, nature-of-mind practice (Theravada), mantra and walking meditation, mindfulness-based stress reduction, Yoga Nidra, visualization practice, Vajrayana tantric meditation, and Samadhi. Qualitative interviews revealed that experts found most pictographic items to be accurate representations of their intended constructs. Based on experts' feedback (see Table S1.2 for details of CQR results in the Supplementary Materials), two changes expanded the MPI: a new item measuring the perception of time slowing down was added, and the original sense-of-self (ego) item was split into two dimensions (hypo-ego and hyper-ego).

Moreover, four items (self-compassion, decentering, self-criticism, and spatial frame of reference continuum) were visually modified to improve clarity and interpretability. As a result, the study developed the first version of the MPI, beginning with 21 items and ultimately expanding to 23 items. The final items are: absorption, body awareness, body boundaries, compassion, connectedness with nature, connectedness with others, decentering, distortion of time: fast, distortion of time: slow, emotional Emotional Reactivity, emotional stability, affect: negative, emotions: positive (note: "emotions" and "affect" will be used indistinctively in the manuscript), ineffability, mental effort, mind wandering, reference continuum, self-compassion, self-criticism, sense-of-self: hypo-ego and hyper-ego, time disappearing, and warmth (see Zenodo repository for the full set of pictographic items, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23449530).

Phase 2 -MPI Validation

The primary objective of Phase 2 was to examine the psychometric properties of the MPI in a general population sample. Specifically, we examined validity evidence based on sensitivity to meditation-induced change, relationship with other variables (including differences between experienced meditators and non-meditators), incremental predictive validity for relevant outcomes, and internal structure, as well as reliability based on temporal and nomological stability.

Single-session meditation practices have been shown to produce measurable changes in affect and state mindfulness (Palmer et al., 2023; Schumer et al., 2018), and are therefore suitable for examining sensitivity to change. We selected three brief practices representing distinct families of meditation: Counting Breath Meditation (CBM), an attentional practice centered on sustained focus and the monitoring of mind wandering; Loving-Kindness Meditation (LKM), a constructive practice aimed at cultivating warmth and care toward oneself and others; and Decentering-Induced Meditation (DIM), which targets the capacity to observe thoughts and feelings as transient mental events. Different contemplative practices have been shown to yield differentiable experiential and psychological profiles (Britton et al., 2018; Przyrembel & Singer, 2018). Psychometric analyses addressed validity evidence based on content, response processes, sensitivity to meditation-induced change, relationship with other variables, incremental predictive validity for relevant outcomes, internal structure, and reliability based on temporal and nomological stability.

The following hypotheses were tested. Hypotheses that were not preregistered are labeled as exploratory; the reasons for the deviations from the preregistration are reported in the Supplementary Materials (Section S2.0). H1 (preregistered). MPI items were expected to form interpretable clusters of related experiences, with positive associations within clusters of similar affective valence (e.g., positive affect, warmth, and compassion) and negative associations between clusters of different affective valence (e.g., negative affect, self-criticism, or emotional Emotional Reactivity).

H2 (preregistered). Compared with the other meditation practice groups, the CBM group was expected to show greater pre-post increases in body awareness and absorption, and greater decreases in mind wandering and mental effort. These items operationalize the preregistered "attentional processes". H3 (preregistered). Compared with the other groups, the LKM group was expected to show greater pre-post increases in compassion, self-compassion, and positive affect. H4 (preregistered). Compared with the other groups, the DIM group was expected to show greater pre-post increases in decentering and greater decreases in emotional Emotional Reactivity.

H5 (preregistered). Compared with non-meditators, experienced meditators were expected to score higher on items of positive experiences and lower on items of negative experiences.

H6 (preregistered). MPI items were expected to show congruent associations with their corresponding self-report measures, correlating positively with conceptually related constructs and negatively with conceptually opposed ones. H7 (not preregistered; exploratory). MPI items were expected to demonstrate incremental predictive validity over established self-reports in predicting emotional dysregulation and positive affect post-meditation. H8 (not preregistered; exploratory). MPI items were expected to show acceptable reliability for single-item measures, operationalized as a test-retest ICC > .40 in the control group (Cicchetti, 1994).

Method Sample and procedure

A total of 378 healthy adults were recruited online from the general population of Spain and Spanish-speaking countries. Inclusion criteria were: i) being 18 years old or older; ii) being able to read and understand the Spanish language; and iii) willingness to participate in the study and sign the written informed consent form. The exclusion criterion was any diagnosis of a disease that may affect the central nervous system (a pathological condition affecting the brain, traumatic brain injury, dementia) or other psychiatric diagnoses or acute psychiatric illnesses (severe range of depression, or other psychotic disorders, eating disorders, psychological trauma), except for anxiety disorder (changed from preregistration, whereas past anxiety was not an exclusion criterion). In total, 1,391 people completed the screening survey; 341 did not meet the inclusion criteria; 665 declined to participate; 4 did not complete the session; and 3 did not respond correctly to control questions. The resulting sample size of 378 participants did not meet our preregistered target (n = 500). Therefore, sensitivity analyses were performed for the implemented analyses, with a general cautionary note that the results might be underpowered. Sensitivity analysis indicated that, in our sample at 95% confidence and 80% power, the minimum detectable effect sizes were d = 0.40, η² p = .063 (main between effect), η² p = .005 (main within effect), η² p = .007 (interaction), r = .14, and R² p = .021. Participants were recruited through various social media platforms (e.g., Instagram, Facebook, etc.) and university newsletters. Screening and consent procedures were conducted via Qualtrics software. All participants signed an informed consent form outlining the aim of the study, the name of the study leader and contact details, and clarifying that they would remain anonymous and that they could withdraw from the study at any time without consequences. To this end, each participant was assigned a code to preserve their confidentiality. Participants were compensated with €10 upon completion of their participation. Participants who met the eligibility criteria were randomly assigned, using an online randomizer tool (https://www.randomizer.org/), to one of four groups: CBM (N = 103); LKM (N = 95); DIM (N = 88); or CG (N = 92) with an audio recording. Before the study session participants filled out demographic questionnaires. The session included the following sequence: i) participants completed pre-meditation state measures, including the MPI; ii) participants listened to the assigned guided meditation or control audio (audio listening of ~ 10 minutes); iii) participants completed post-meditation state measures, including the MPI.

Study sessions lasted one hour and were conducted via Zoom. Participants were required to keep their cameras on and join via a computer (mobile phones were not allowed, as smaller screens could compromise optimal visualization of the MPI items). They were instructed to enter the Zoom call using the unique code assigned to them beforehand.

Instruments

All instruments were administered in Spanish. When only an English version was available, questionnaires were translated ad hoc using a forward-backward translation procedure (Beaton et al., 2000): two bilingual researchers independently translated the items into Spanish, a native English speaker blind to the original back-translated them, and discrepancies were resolved by consensus.

Sociodemographic and meditation experience.

Participants were asked about some demographics (Table 1), their experience with meditation (yes/no), estimated duration of practices, length of interruptions in their habit for practice, and the proportion of time spent on each type (concentration-based, open monitoring, compassion/loving-kindness, values, deconstructive/non-duality, and informal practice). Seven participants reported having experience but also reported no practice per week at all, thus were allocated in the non-meditator group. Prior to the session, participants filled in baseline self-reports. During the session, participants completed various state questionnaires at both pre-and post-meditation.

Measurements administered at both pre-and post-meditation were the following: Meditation Pictographic Inventory (MPI). This inventory measures meditation-related experiences. It consists of 23 pictographic items with a Likert response format from 1 ("Not at all") to 7 ("Very much"). Each item is a single-item measure of a specific experience. They were preceded by a brief definition of the experiential construct to ensure clarity. At baseline (pre), the question was: "Which of these images best represents your level of [concept] right now?" After the meditation (post), it was: "Which of these images best represents your level of [concept] while you were listening to the audio?". Post-meditation ratings were therefore retrospective reports of the session, collected immediately after it.

Nondual Awareness Dimensional Assessment (NADA-S; Hanley et al., 2018; ad hoc

Spanish translation (PQ-M e IME)). This scale was developed to measure experiential effects of nondual awareness and non-attachment, such as self-transcendence (a state in which the usual distinction between self and the environment dissolves, leading to a sense of unity, interconnectedness, and a reduced sense of ego). It consists of 3 items and is scored on a 10-point Likert scale from 1 ("Not at all") to 10 ("Very much"). Internal consistency was adequate (α =.90).

State Mindfulness scale (SMS; Tanay & Bernstein, 2013; validated for the Spanish population by Navarrete et al., 2023). This scale measures mindfulness states. It consists of 21 items with a Likert response format from 1 ("Not at all") to 5 ("Very well"). Internal consistencies were good (α =.94 and .86). Neff et al., 2021; validated to the Spanish population by Galiana et al., 2022). This scale measures state self-compassion. It consists of 18 items with a Likert response format from 1 ("Strongly disagree") to 5 ("Strongly agree").

Internal consistency ranged from poor to acceptable (α = .55-.79).

Short other-compassion scale (S-OCS).

This instrument was adapted from the self-compassion state scale (Neff et al., 2021) to measure other-compassion rather than self-compassion. It consists of 5 items with a Likert response format from 1 ("not at all true in me") to 5 ("very true in me"). Internal consistency was between questionable and fair (α = .63 and .75). Roca et al., 2023). This scale measures arousal (high and low) and valence (positive and negative), although in this study only valence was used for simplicity. It consists of 12 items with a Likert response format from 1 ("Not at all") to 4 ("Extremely"). The original version of this questionnaire was developed in Spanish. The scale demonstrated acceptable internal consistencies (α = .75 -.78).

Hedonic and Arousal Affect Scale (HAAS; Original version in Spanish,

State Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (S-DERS; Lavender et al., 2017).

Spanish item wording was taken from the validated Spanish version of the trait DERS (Hervás & Jódar, 2008) and adapted to state format following Lavender et al. (2017). This scale measures difficulties in emotion self-regulation, or an emotion dysregulation state. It consists of 17 items with a Likert response format from 1 ("Almost never") to 5 ("Almost always").

Internal consistencies were mostly acceptable (α = .62 to .89).

Experience questionnaire (EQ; Fresco et al., 2007; validated for the Spanish population by Soler et al., 2014). We used the 11-item decentering subscale with instructions adapted to refer to the present moment (e.g., "Right now…"), to assess state decentering, that is, the momentary capacity to observe one's thoughts and feelings as transient mental events. Items were rated on a Likert scale from 1 ("Never") to 5 ("All the time"). Internal consistency was good (α = .85).

Three additional measures were administered only post-meditation as experimental checks and adverse effect of meditation assessment for the specific meditation practice:

In the CBM and DIM group: The Practice quality-mindfulness scale (PQ-M; Del Re et al., 2013; ad hoc Spanish translation (PQ-M e IME)), to evaluate the quality of the meditation session. It consists of 6 items ranging from 0% to 100%. Internal consistency was questionable (α = .59).

In the LKM group: The Quality of the Practice of Compassion Scale (CPQS; Original version in Spanish, Navarrete et al., 2021), to evaluate the quality of the compassionate meditation session. This scale consists of 18 items, with Likert responses ranging from 0% to 100%. Internal consistency was acceptable (α = .88). (IME; Van Dam et al., 2024; ad hoc Spanish translation). This scale measures several experiences related to meditation practices considered unusual. It consists of 30 items with a Likert response format from 1 ("Not at all") to 6 ("Extreme"), grouped into 3 factors (enabling experiences, disabling experiences, and distortions in self/reality). Internal consistency was acceptable to excellent across factors (α = .75-.92).

Inventory of Meditation Experiences

Data analysis

Baseline characteristics.

Descriptive statistics were computed for the sample's sociodemographic variables, and self-reports. The MPI item distributions were inspected graphically. Baseline differences between groups were examined using one-way ANOVAs for continuous variables (e.g., age, level of education), and chi-square tests for categorical variables (e.g., gender, marital status).

The same comparisons were conducted for MPI items and self-reports at baseline, using robust or non-parametric alternatives when assumptions were not met. The latent structure of non-MPI self-reports was examined through Confirmatory Factor Analyses (CFAs, see Section S2.1 in the Supplementary Materials for details of the data analysis).

Internal structure-based validity.

Since the MPI does not conform to reflective or formative models (each item is conceived as a distinct, item-level construct), a psychometric network approach was chosen, as it assumes items are unique variables rather than latent constructs (Borsboom et al., 2021; Isvoranu et al., 2022). Moreover, a loading comparison test suggested that psychometric networks were more appropriate than factor models (Christensen & Golino, 2021). Thus, for both theoretical and empirical reasons, we deviated from preregistration, following established methodological guidelines (Lakens, 2024).

To ensure the stability of the findings, a priori hoc power and replicability analyses were conducted (Epskamp et al., 2018; Supplementary Materials, Section S2.2, Figures S1-S2). They indicated around 80% sensitivity, 99% specificity, 80% replicated non-zero edges, and 95% replicated zero edges. A non-regularized estimation method (ggmModSelect) was selected along with polychoric correlations, given its higher sparsity (minimizing unnecessary connections), sensitivity and specificity in edge detection (Isvoranu & Epskamp, 2023). The network was screened for potential biases, including i) non-informative nodes (low variability), ii) outlier response patterns, iii) collinear pairs, and iv) collider bias. None of these biases or technical issues were found. Network node predictability was assessed using the R² statistic.

To estimate clusters of items, Exploratory Graph Analysis (EGA; Golino & Epskamp, 2017) was employed using both the walktrap and Louvain community detection algorithms and the resulting solutions were compared using fit indices (Christensen et al., 2024; Golino et al., 2020; Golino et al., 2021). Although EGA communities can correspond to latent factors, MPI items are conceptualized as item-level constructs. EGA outcomes were therefore interpreted as descriptive groupings of related experiences rather than as latent constructs: the item remains the primary unit of measurement and interpretation, whereas clusters were used to summarize results and to estimate aggregate reliability. Node centrality was interpreted using strength and bridge strength (Jones et al., 2021), as other indices (e.g., closeness, betweenness) did not reach acceptable stability and their interpretation in psychological networks has been questioned (Bringmann et al., 2019). Bootstrapping was applied to assess the stability of edges, clusters, and centrality indices. Note that based on its observed association pattern and EGA (see Results), the emotional stability item was reverse-coded and renamed "emotional instability" for all subsequent analyses, this decision was data-driven and not preregistered.

To examine change over time, the three meditation groups were pooled and the preand post-intervention networks were compared through network invariance analysis (metric invariance tested with Benjamini-Hochberg correction; Jamison et al., 2024) and the paired Network Comparison Test (van Borkulo et al., 2023), with edge-wise tests also BH-corrected.

Because pre-and post-are repeated measures, each occasion's network was estimated independently, which is unbiased for each cross-sectional structure, while inference on differences relied on the within-person permutation of the paired NCT; the Fused Graphical Lasso (Costantini et al., 2019), which assumes independent groups, was retained only as a descriptive sensitivity analysis. Group-level network comparisons were not explored due to limited statistical power (n ≈ 100 per group).

Effects of the three meditation practices on the MPI items.

To assess the MPI's sensitivity to change induced by the three meditation practices as compared to control condition, a 4 (group: CBM, LKM, DIM, CG) × 2 (time: pre, post) mixed ANCOVA was conducted. Each MPI item was used as the dependent variable. Meditation experience was used as covariate. Assumptions were checked, and corrections or robust alternatives were implemented. Post hoc comparisons were used with Holm-Bonferroni correction alongside marginal means with their confidence intervals. A manipulation check was performed on state self-reports to assess impact of meditations. The same analysis was performed but without covariates and state self-reports as dependent variables. In addition, relations between MPI and meditation experience were assessed using Mann-Whitney tests.

Correction for multiple comparisons across items was not applied for two reasons. First, family-wise error control is not applicable because each item is regarded as measuring a different construct (like in standard RCTs with several self-reports). Second, correcting across 23 tests would reduce statistical power excessively for practically useful inferences. Consistent with an estimation-based approach (Cumming, 2014), confidence intervals of estimated marginal means were interpreted alongside F-tests: convergent results were regarded as consistent evidence, and divergent results as mixed evidence.

External variables-based validity.

Associations between MPI items and relevant constructs were examined using Spearman correlations, with graphical checks for linearity and outliers. Pre-and post-MPI measurements were correlated with their respective pre-and post-self-report measurements. To examine the prospective predictive capability of the MPI items, two families of 23 hierarchical multiple regression analyses were conducted, one per dependent variable: emotional dysregulation (S-DERS) and positive affect (HAAS-p), both measured post-intervention. For each MPI item (pre), three nested models were compared: M0, a null model; M1, group (dummy-coded) and content-matched self-report covariates at pre-(see Table S5 in the Supplementary Materials); and M2 the MPI item. Selection criteria for self-reports were done by theoretical correspondence, established nomological networks in meditation research, minimizing collinearity, and based on the co-authors consensus (not preregistered; see Supplementary Materials, Section S2.0 and S2.7 for details). The group variable was included to control for treatment-related variance in the outcomes. R² change and the standardized slope of the item were reported, with p-value corrected by Benjamini-Hochberg within each family, along 95% bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) confidence intervals obtained via case bootstrapping (5,000 resamples, stratified by intervention group; percentile intervals were used when the R² change approached zero). Assumptions were checked and are reported in Supplementary Materials, Section S2.7 (Table S7); the full analysis is available in Zenodo repository. Finally, a sensitivity analysis added the baseline (pre) score of each dependent variable to M1, testing whether the items predicted change beyond baseline stability rather than future levels (Supplementary Materials, Section S2.7, Table S6)

Single-item reliability.

To examine reliability, temporal stability was used as the main source due to single-item measures (Allen et al., 2022; Geusens et al. 2022; Song et al., 2023; Bagaïni et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2024). Only the control group was used to compute these indices due to manipulation. Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC 3,1 , with values > .40 as acceptable; Cicchetti, 1994) were estimated for each item, along with Standard Error of Difference (SED), the Minimum Detectable Change (MDC) indices, and the percentage of participants in meditation groups that surpassed the MDCs. Bland-Altman plots were screened for a more detailed examination (Supplementary Materials, Figure S7). In addition, criterion-based temporal stability (i.e., nomological stability) was regarded as a source of reliability (Feng et al., 2024; also noted as nomological stability). It was estimated using the attenuation correction formula (Spearman, 1904):

Where is the estimated reliability of the item, is the correlation between the item 𝑟 correlation under which each item would hold an acceptable reliability for ICC-type coefficients (Cicchetti, 1994). Because the averaged criterion reliability was nearly constant (α ≈ .86), these two quantities can reproduce the curves.

Finally, Generalizability Theory (G-Theory; Cronbach et al., 1972; Brennan, 2001) was used to estimate the reliability of aggregated cluster scores. Unlike classical reliability coefficients, G-theory decomposes measurement error into multiple sources (facets) and estimates the contribution of each through variance components (Southam-Gerow et al., 2020).

We specified a random-effects design in which persons were nested in groups and crossed with items and time, (p:g) x i x t, yielding eleven variance components (main effects, two-and three-way interactions, and the residual), estimated via REML (Bates et al., 2015). At the cluster level, items were treated as a sample of related experiences rather than as interchangeable indicators of a latent construct. Item and time-related components were therefore treated as sources of error, so that the indices report the extent to which differences between persons in aggregated cluster scores generalize across items and time. Two indices were computed: a generalizability coefficient (G), for relative comparisons (e.g., ranking individuals), whose error term comprises only interactions involving persons, and a dependability coefficient (Φ) for absolute comparisons (e.g., interpreting score levels as high or low), whose error term additionally includes item-, time-, and group-related interactions. In addition, because this design addresses the consistency of cluster scores but not their relations with external variables, a complementary G-index was computed to assess nomological stability at the cluster level, consistent with the criterion-based approach described above.

Fisher Z-transformed item-criterion correlations were treated as observations of a single-facet crossed design, with item × criterion pairs as objects of measurement and time (pre-and post-) as the error facet. The resulting index, one per cluster, is formally equivalent to an ICC between the pre-and post-correlation profiles and indicates how reproducible each cluster's pattern of relations with external criteria is over time. Only criteria administered at both occasions were included in the analysis. All G-theory indices are reported as overall measures complementary to the item-level evidence.

Analyses were computed using JASP software (JASP team, 2026) and the R statistical environment (R Core Team, 2024). The main packages implemented were lavaan (Rosseel, 2011), psych (Revelle, 2024), bootnet (Epskamp et al., 2018), networktools (Jones & Jones, 2020), EGAnet (Golino & Christensen, 2024), NetworkComparisonTest (van Borkulo et al., 2023), EstimateGroupNetwork (Costantini et al., 2019), responsepatterns (Gottfried et al., 2022), lme4 (Bates et al., 2015), boot (Canty & Ripley, 2025) and ggplot2 (Wickham, 2016).

This study was preregistered. Data, analysis code, and all materials, including the pictographic items are openly available in the Zenodo repository Results are organized as follows. First, we report baseline characteristics of the sample.

Second, we report internal-structure evidence (H1), including the network structure of the MPI, its stability, and its comparison from pre to post, followed by descriptive statistics of the items.

Third, we report the manipulation check on state self-reports, followed by the sensitivity of MPI items to the three meditation practices (H2-H4) and differences between experienced and inexperienced meditators (H5). Fourth, we report validity evidence based on relations with other variables, including correlations with self-reports (H6) and incremental prediction of post-meditation outcomes (H7). Finally, we report single-item and cluster-level reliability (H8).

Results

Baseline characteristics

The general characteristics of the participants are shown in Table 1. The demographics analysis indicates no significant differences between groups across all variables, indicating that the groups were comparable on most baseline variables. The only exception was the level of education (F(3,335) = 3.1, p = .028, η²p = .027), which was slightly lower in the LKM group compared to the others. Given the small effect, it was not included as a covariate, to limit researcher degrees of freedom. All groups were mostly females (80.5%), White (84.7%), single (45.1%), and students (55.7%). About 41% of the participants reported some experience with meditation, with an average of 2 years and typical practice sessions of approximately 25 minutes/day. The item originally named "emotional stability", initially conceived as positive experience, correlated negatively with items in the positive cluster and positively with items in the negative cluster. Thus, this item did not seem to fit the expected cluster. Consequently, to enhance interpretability and consistency, the item was reversed and renamed "emotional instability" in the final version of the MPI.

Edges were predominantly positive. Negative edges connected the positive and negative clusters, including expected pairs (e.g., positive and negative affect; emotional instability with positive affect, body awareness, and decentering; body awareness with ineffability). Within the heterogeneous cluster, hypo-ego and hyper-ego were also negatively connected.

Regarding centrality (Figure 2), emotional instability showed the highest strength, followed by positive affect. Emotional instability was strongly connected within the negative cluster and negatively connected with positive affect. Positive affect, in turn, showed a strong edge with warmth and a negative edge with emotional instability, so that its strength derived more from between-cluster than within-cluster connections. The same pattern emerged for bridge strength: emotional instability linked the negative and positive clusters, whereas positive affect was more connected with the negative cluster than with its own. Compassion and time disappearing also showed relatively high, though lower, strength and bridge strength. Note. Blue circles indicate the positive cluster, red circles represent the negative cluster, and yellow circles correspond to the heterogeneous cluster. Blue lines denote positive correlations, while red lines indicate negative correlations. The thickness of the lines reflects the strength of the correlations.

Network stability and replicability

To assess the stability of the network estimates, including edges, centrality indices, and cluster assignments, we performed bootstrapping analyses ( Note. Intervals are 95% bootstrapped confidence intervals. Network comparison across time (pre -post) To examine whether the structure identified at baseline changed after meditation, the three meditation groups were pooled and the networks at pre and post were compared. Metric invariance tests suggested lower network loadings at pre for some nodes, but no difference remained after applying Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) correction. The paired Network Comparison Test indicated invariant global structure and global strength; no edge-wise differences remained after applying BH correction, and node centrality did not differ significantly. The networks estimated independently at each occasion are shown in Figure 3.

Thus, H1 was partially supported: the positive and negative clusters were internally coherent and connected mainly through negative edges, whereas the heterogeneous cluster was not coherent. Thus, no significant differences in network structure emerged from pre to post, in contrast with the mean-level changes reported below. Given the sample size and the absence of equivalence tests, this indicates no evidence of structural change rather than demonstrated invariance (see Section "Effects of the three meditation practices on the MPI items" in the Results). Descriptive statistics of MPI items

Figure 4 shows the density distributions and medians of MPI items by group and time point and Table S2.3 in the Supplementary Materials reports detailed descriptive statistics.

Most items in the positive cluster tended to score above the scale midpoint (except body boundaries and reference continuum at pre), items in the negative cluster below it, and items in the heterogeneous cluster showed mixed patterns across groups and time points. Relative to the CG, meditation groups showed significant differences at post on state mindfulness, emotion dysregulation, nondual awareness, and decentering (Figure S3 and details in the Zenodo repository). Neither state self-compassion (S-SCS) nor state other-compassion (S-OCS) showed significant Group × Time interactions, including for LKM.

At post, groups also differed on the IME (measuring unusual meditation experiences, specifically enabling and distortion factors, but not on disabling experience). Practice quality was assessed with different instruments across groups (CPQS for LKM; PQ-M for CBM and DIM).

CPQS is therefore reported descriptively, whereas PQ-M was compared between CBM and DIM with Welch's t-test and is reported through estimates and 95% CIs (Figure S3 in the Supplementary Materials).

Sensitivity of MPI items to the three meditation practices

Sensitivity to change was examined through 4 (Group: CBM, LKM, DIM, CG) × 2 (Time: pre -post) mixed ANCOVAs, with meditation experience as an exploratory covariate.

Two effects are reported. First, previous meditation experience showed a significant main effect on 13 of the 23 items (Supplementary Materials, Section S2.6, FigureS5), most strongly on emotional Emotional Reactivity (η²p = .32), emotional instability (η²p = .11), and negative affect (η²p = .09), indicating overall differences in levels between experienced and inexperienced participants. Second, the Time × Experience interaction, reflecting differences in pre-post change, was significant for reference continuum, emotional Emotional Reactivity, positive affect, and negative affect. Significant Group × Time interactions emerged for nine of the 23 items (Supplementary Materials, Section S2.5, Table S4). No significant interaction was found for the remaining 14 items (all p ≥ .05), including compassion, connectedness with others, decentering, emotional Emotional Reactivity, self-criticism, and negative affect. Post hoc comparisons revealed two patterns.

General effects of meditation compared to CG. At post-meditation, all three meditation groups scored higher than the CG on body awareness, F(3, 373) = 12.40, p < .001, η²p = .09; body boundaries (i.e., greater dissolution, F(3, 373) = 7.64, p < .001, η²p = .06); reference continuum, F(3, 373) = 6.58, p < .001, η²p = .05; and time disappearing, F(3, 373) = 5.55, p < .001, η²p = .04, without differing from one another. These items therefore captured changes common to the three practices.

Practice-specific effects. LKM produced higher scores than the other three groups on self-compassion, F(3, 373) = 10.80, p < .001, η²p = .08; positive affect, F(3, 373) = 3.71, p < .05, η²p = .03; and warmth, F(3, 373) = 6.52, p < .001, η²p = .05. DIM also produced higher self-compassion scores than the CG and CBM. Interactions were also significant for mind wandering, F(3, 373) = 4.59, p < .01, η²p = .04, and mental effort, F(3, 373) = 3.57, p < .05, η²p = .03 in the expected directions. In contrast, items of the negative cluster decreased markedly over time in all groups, including the CG (e.g., emotional Emotional Reactivity, F(1, 373) = 235.52, p < .001, η²p = .39), without group differences. Contrary to H2, CBM did not differ from the other meditation groups in body awareness or mind wandering; contrary to H4, DIM did not specifically increase decentering or reduce emotional Emotional Reactivity. No significant interaction was found for absorption, connectedness with nature, hypo-ego, and hyper-ego. Accordingly, H3 was partially supported: LKM produced specific increases in self-compassion, positive affect, and warmth, but not in compassion. Figure 5 displays means and 95% CIs by group and time (details also available at Figure S4).

To assess differences between experienced meditators and inexperienced individuals, Mann-Whitney tests were conducted. The results indicated that experienced meditators reported significantly lower levels of mind wandering, emotional instability, mental effort, time fast, ineffability, Emotional Reactivity, negative affect, and hyper-ego (all p < .05). Moreover, they showed higher levels of self-compassion, compassion, connectedness with nature, decentering, positive affect, body awareness, and warmth (all p < .05). This pattern largely mirrors the main effect of experience in the ANCOVAs. The minor differences (self-criticism differed only in the ANCOVAs; body awareness, time fast, and hyper-ego only in the Mann-Whitney tests) likely reflect that the ANCOVA effect is adjusted for group and averaged across time points. These results support H5. Note. Values are estimated marginal means from the mixed ANCOVAs, adjusted for meditation experience. Cluster scores were computed as the mean of the items in each cluster. Scores of negative-cluster items and of the negative cluster score were inverted for display purposes, so that higher values indicate more favorable experiences across all axes. Confidence intervals are uncorrected; consistent with the estimation-based approach adopted (see Data analysis), inference is based on confidence intervals together with Holm-corrected post hoc comparisons (Table S4, Supplementary Materials). Abbreviations: S-comp = self-compassion; Positive emo = positive affect, S-other = connectedness with others, S-nature = connectedness with nature, Mental eff = mental effort, Time disap = time disappearing.

External variables-based validity: Correlations with self-reports

Figure 6 shows Spearman correlations between MPI items and state self-report at pre-and post. Overall, correlations followed the expected direction (H6).

At pre-meditation, state mindfulness (SMS), state self-compassion (S-SCS), decentering (EQ), nondual awareness (NADA-S), and positive affect (HAAS) correlated positively with positive-cluster items, most consistently with positive affect, warmth, self-compassion, and compassion (r ≈ .15-.25, all p < .05), and negatively with emotional Emotional Reactivity, negative affect, and self-criticism (r ≈ -.12 to -.22, all p < .05).

Emotion dysregulation (S-DERS) showed the strongest associations: positive with mind wandering, mental effort, emotional Emotional Reactivity, negative affect, emotional instability, and self-criticism (r = .25-.35, all p <.05) and negative with self-compassion, compassion, positive affect, warmth, connectedness with others, and reference continuum (r ≈ .20, all p < .05).

Negative affect (HAAS) mirrored the pattern of positive affect. Two exceptions emerged: state other-compassion (S-OCS) correlated with compassion-related items but not negatively with negative-cluster items, and mind wandering was unrelated to state mindfulness.

At post-meditation, this pattern was largely replicated, although some self-reports correlated only with positive cluster items (S-OCS at both time points, S-SCS at post, and NADA-S at pre). Among the IME factors, measured only at post, enabling experiences and distortions in self showed congruent associations, whereas disabling experiences correlated (positively) only with negative-cluster items. Taken together, correlations followed the expected direction at both time points, although most were small to moderate (r ≈ .15-.35), providing initial but modest convergent evidence. H6 was therefore supported in direction. Note. *p < .05, **p < .01, ***p < .001.

External variables-based validity: Multiple Regression Analyses over emotional dysregulation and positive affect

Hierarchical regressions tested whether each MPI item at pre predicted post-intervention emotion dysregulation (S-DERS) and positive affect (HAAS-p) beyond group and content-matched self-reports at pre (Table S5). After Benjamini-Hochberg correction, 12 of the 23 MPI items showed significant incremental prediction of post-intervention emotional dysregulation, and 14 of 23 predicted post-intervention positive affect (Figure 7; full coefficients in Zenodo repository; all confidence intervals are BCa unless noted).

Incremental effects were largest for the negative-cluster items: emotional instability showed the strongest effects (S-DERS, ΔR² = .16, 95% CI [.09, .23], β = .41 [.31, .49];

HAAS-p: ΔR² = .10 [.05, .16], β = -.33 [-.42, -.23]) followed by self-criticism (S-DERS: ΔR² = .14 [.09, .21], β = .39 [.31, .47]), with all seven negative-cluster items significant for both outcomes.

Positive-cluster items predicted positive affect more consistently (7 of 11 significantly, led by Self-Compassion and Warmth, both β = .31 [.22, .40]) than emotional dysregulation (3 of 11).

29

Heterogeneous-cluster items showed only small effects, limited to emotional dysregulation (Time slow and Hyper-ego, ΔR² ≈ .03).

The sensitivity analysis adding the baseline score of each dependent variable to the covariate block nullified all incremental effects (all ΔR² ≤ .01, all BH-corrected p ≥ .05), indicating that the items predict future levels of the outcomes largely through their association with concurrent baseline standing, rather than predicting change beyond baseline stability (Supplementary Materials, Section S2.7, Table S6). H7 was thus supported for future levels of the outcomes, but not for change.
