Single-item Reliability

Table 2 summarizes all reliability evidence (plots are available at Supplementary Materials, Section S2.8, Figure S7-S9). Following Cicchetti (1994), test-retest stability in the control group was poor for 11 items (ICC(3,1) = .21-.39), and fair for 11 items (ICC = .41-.50), with only Hyper-Ego, showing good stability (ICC = .73 [.62, .81]). Consistent with these single-item ICCs, minimum detectable changes were large (MDC₉₅ = 2.25-4.54 points on the 1-7 scale), and only a minority of participants in the meditation groups showed change exceeding the minimum detectable changes in the expected direction (0.3%-14.7% per item, largest for Mind-Wandering, Time Slow, and Hyper-Ego). Criterion-based reliability floors (the most conservative estimate, obtained under the assumption of a perfect true item-criterion correlation) ranged from .00 to .21, being higher for positive-cluster items (e.g., Warmth = .21 [.13, .29] and Reference Continuum = .17 [.10, .25] at post) and near zero for the heterogeneous cluster.

The ρ(.40) index showed a similar gradient: several positive items reached fair reliability even under relatively high assumed true correlations (ρ = .50-.72), negative items under intermediate values (ρ ≈ .23-.56), and heterogeneous items only under values close to their observed correlations (ρ ≤ .20, except Time Disappearing at post, ρ = .40).

Cluster-level G-theory indices followed the same gradient: generalizability and dependability were good for the positive cluster (G = .68, Φ = .63), good and fair, respectively, for the negative cluster (G = .61, Φ = .49), and fair and poor for the heterogeneous cluster (G = .43, Φ = .36). Finally, the nomological-stability indices indicated that the pattern of item-criterion correlations was highly reproducible from pre-to post-for the positive (G_nomol = .93) and negative (G_nomol = .89) clusters, and less so for the heterogeneous cluster (G_nomol = .55). H8 was therefore partially supported: 12 of 23 items exceeded the preset ICC threshold of .40, and positive and negative cluster scores showed good relative reliability. (cluster) G = .43 Φ = .36 G nomol = . decisions) and Φ = dependability coefficient (absolute decisions); G nomol = nomological-stability coefficient for cluster's pattern of item-criterion correlations.

General Discussion

This study developed the Meditation Pictographic Inventory (MPI), a set of 23 pictographic single-item measures of meditation-related experiential states, and provided preliminary validity evidence through a multi-source framework combining evidence on content, response processes, sensitivity to change, relations with other variables, incremental prediction, internal structure, and reliability. Taken together, the findings suggest that pictographic single-items are a feasible complement to verbal self-reports for assessing meditation experiences. However, the evidence is uneven across items. Some items showed converging support from most sources (warmth, positive emotions, emotional instability, body awareness, body boundaries, compassion, self-compassion, reference continuum, time disappearing). Others, particularly those concerning time perception and the sense of self, require future revision. Support for the hypotheses was mixed. H1 (internal structure) was partially supported: a three-cluster network structure (positive, negative, heterogeneous) emerged, but only the positive and negative clusters were internally coherent. Three items (body boundaries, absorption, and ineffability) showed unstable cluster membership. H2 was not supported as formulated: CBM did not specifically change body awareness or mind wandering. H3 was partially supported: LKM produced the highest scores on self-compassion, positive affect, and warmth, but not compassion or connectedness with others. H4 was not supported: DIM did not specifically increase decentering or reduce emotional Emotional Reactivity. H5 was supported: experienced meditators differed from non-meditators across multiple items, although these differences are correlational rather than causal, as meditation experience was not manipulated.

H6 was supported in direction, although most associations were small: at both pre-and post-meditation, MPI items correlated positively with conceptually related self-reports and negatively with conceptually opposed ones. H7 (exploratory) was not supported for change.

Although 12 and 14 of the 23 items predicted post-meditation emotion dysregulation and positive affect, respectively, beyond group and content-matched self-reports, adding the baseline score of each outcome eliminated all incremental effects (all ΔR² ≤ .005). The items therefore predicted future levels through their association with concurrent baseline standing, rather than change. The largest effects were observed for negative-cluster items, especially emotional instability and self-criticism, which is partly expected given their content overlap with emotion dysregulation; because emotional instability was reinterpreted and reverse-coded post hoc, its interpretation requires independent confirmation. H8 was partially supported: 12 of 23 items exceeded the preset ICC threshold, and positive and negative cluster scores reached good relative reliability, whereas heterogeneous items remained unreliable on most indices.

Network structure of the MPI

As described in the Method, psychometric networks were preferred over latent-variable models because MPI items are conceived as distinct single-item measures rather than interchangeable indicators of a common factor, a choice also supported by the loading comparison test (Christensen & Golino, 2021). The resulting network showed a moderately stable structure with three clusters of items (positive, negative, and heterogeneous).

Positive Cluster. The first cluster identified in the network analysis includes items measuring pleasant or positively regarded meditation experiences, such as warmth, compassion, and positive affect. However, some items included in this cluster (body awareness, decentering, absorption, and reference continuum) are affectively neutral rather than explicitly positive. Despite their neutrality, previous research suggests that these experiences may be associated with well-being (Dambrun, 2016; Vidal et al., 2026b). Notably, bootstrapped EGA showed low item stability for body boundaries and absorption, indicating that their assignment to the positive cluster was inconsistent across resamples. This suggests that while these states may not be strongly interconnected with the other positive experiences in the network, they could still play a facilitative role in meditation, serving as fundamental states that enable or enhance other positive experiences, such as compassion and positive affect.

Negative Cluster. The second cluster includes items that measure unpleasant or negative meditation-related experiences, such as emotional Emotional Reactivity and mind wandering. Mind wandering was clustered with negative experiences, consistent with its frequent association with negative mood, although its affective consequences are not uniformly negative (Mason et al., 2013). Notably, ineffability was also grouped within this cluster, which is unexpected given that much of the literature conceptualizes ineffability as a neutral or even a positive mental state (Gäb, 2024). Several explanations may account for this classification.

Firstly, the pictographic representation of ineffability depicts a meditator with speech balloons containing the word "Bla" ranging from multiple balloons to none. Some participants may have interpreted this image as representing mind wandering rather than an inability to articulate an experience, which could explain its alignment with negative experiences. Secondly, ineffability is not inherently a hedonic state (Ji et al., 2024); its emotional valence may depend on its relationship with other experiential factors, such as connection to others or nature. Further research is needed to clarify whether ineffability carries a predominantly positive, negative, or context-dependent affective dimension, particularly in the context of meditation.

Heterogeneous Cluster. The third remaining cluster encompasses items related to distortions in time perception and the self, including hypo-and hyper-ego states, although it does not behave as a coherent cluster, given its weak correlations and unstable properties. It was labeled "Heterogeneous" because it encompasses a varied set of states regarding time perception and changes in ego boundaries with unstable structure, connections between them, and with other constructs. Interestingly, the connection between the positive and heterogeneous clusters appears to be mediated through items measuring the spatial frame of reference and body dissolution. This finding aligns with literature, which often conceptualizes selflessness as an experiential overlap between altered self-perception and expanded awareness (Canby et al., 2024; Vidal et al., 2026b). Indeed, "selflessness" was considered as a name for this cluster, although it was ultimately rejected since some of its core components (e.g., body awareness, ineffability) were located in other clusters. Further research is needed to allocate selflessness in the MPI. Moreover, this cluster may hold particular relevance for psychedelic research, given that distortions in time perception and self-awareness are commonly reported in such altered states. Previous versions of these items were used in a selflessness induction in virtual reality (Vidal et al., 2026b), where they showed sensitivity to expanded states of consciousness. This suggests that the MPI may be a useful tool for investigating both meditative and non-ordinary states of awareness.

To further explore the temporal dynamics of meditative experiences, we examined how their relationships changed across pre-and post-meditation states. Network comparisons did not reveal significant differences between pre and post, suggesting that the MPI changed at the mean level without detectable reorganization of its structure. However, non-significant differences do not demonstrate invariance, and the change in the temporal reference of the items between pre and post (current state vs. retrospective report of the session) may have influenced both mean levels and associations. Equivalence tests in larger samples are needed to establish structural stability.

Effects of the Meditation Practices on MPI Items

While meditation practices generally influenced participants' experiences, the patterns of change varied across types of meditation practices. Nine of the 23 items showed significant Group x Time interactions, supporting the sensitivity of a subset of MPI items to brief meditation practices. Positive experiences, such as self-compassion, warmth, and positive affect, increased especially with LKM, whereas negative experiences, such as emotional Emotional Reactivity and self-criticism decreased significantly in all groups. The other heterogeneous experiences, such as time perception shifts and changes in self-boundaries, exhibited mixed or non-significant patterns. Thus, a subset of MPI items appears sensitive to meditation-related change, whereas the decrease in negative-cluster items was not specific to meditation (see below). Interestingly, some experiential dimensions appeared to be more consistently modulated by meditation than others. MPI items related to body awareness, body boundaries, reference continuum, and time disappearing showed consistent changes across meditation groups relative to CG, without differences among practices, suggesting that these experiences may be common to the brief practices tested, regardless of practice type, particularly those related to bodily experience and the sense of self (Canby et al., 2024).

The results also suggest that the MPI was sensitive to specific impacts of some practice.

As hypothesized (H3), the MPI detected LKM-specific increases in self-compassion, positive affect, and warmth. However, compassion and connectedness with others, also expected to increase in LKM, showed no significant interaction. Contrary to H2 and H4, CBM did not specifically increase body awareness or absorption, or reduce mind wandering, and DIM did not specifically increase decentering or reduce emotional Emotional Reactivity. DIM, however, produced higher self-compassion than CG and CBM. Mind wandering and mental effort also showed significant interactions. However, the LKM-specific increase in self-compassion was not mirrored by the corresponding verbal self-reports (S-SCS), which did not differ from the control group. This divergence may indicate that these changes require more prolonged practice, that the MPI self-compassion item partly captures warmth or positive affect (see below), or that the verbal measure was less sensitive to brief state changes, particularly given the questionable internal consistency of the S-SCS. Overall, these findings support several MPI items as sensitive tools for capturing diverse meditative states and provide further evidence that different meditation practices elicit distinct experiential profiles (Singer & Engert, 2019).

Future research should explore whether longer meditation training, individual differences, or specific practice meditation contribute to these effects, particularly regarding distortions in time and self-perception, which appear to be more variable across individuals.

Items of the negative cluster (e.g., emotional Emotional Reactivity, self-criticism, and negative affect) decreased markedly over time in all groups, including the CG, without group differences. This suggests that these changes could reflect the session context (e.g., relaxation, familiarization, or regression to the mean) rather than meditation-specific effects, and that these items may require stronger or longer interventions to detect practice-specific change.

Some items (absorption, self-nature connectedness, time fast, time slow, hypo-ego, hyper-ego) did not show statistically significant differences. Compassion and connectedness with others also showed no significant interaction, which is unexpected, as previous research suggests that loving-kindness meditation increases feelings of social connectedness (Hutcherson et al., 2008). For connectedness with others, LKM showed higher scores than the other groups, but this difference did not differ from pre to post and may therefore reflect pre-existing group differences rather than an effect of the practice. This is unexpected, as theoretical frameworks (e.g., Neff et al., 2021) point to the presence of these effects, particularly in compassion and self-other connection. A potential explanation would be induction via short meditation (e.g., Górska & Holas, 2025), the lower reliability of some of these items, or both. Given the exploratory outlook of this study, future research should test the MPI in other samples to explore in more depth these results. Specifically, standardized meditation programs (e.g., MBSR, MBCT, MSC) could improve the quality of interventions regarding the properties of the MPI, offering a clearer estimate of item sensitivity. These results suggest that some core effects of meditation, particularly those related to self-processing and body awareness, are present even in novice practitioners, independent of specific meditation content. This finding is of particular interest, since these items reflect changes in selflessness, a phenomenon that has often been overlooked in meditation research (Canby et al., 2024; Vidal et al., 2026a) but has gained renewed attention in the context of adverse effects of meditation (Van Dam et al., 2024) and psychedelic research (e.g., Kałużna et al., 2022).

Two items exhibited distinct response patterns that warrant further examination. Firstly, the emotional stability item correlated with negative affect items, suggesting it may capture emotional instability rather than stability. However, interpreting emotional instability solely as a negative state may be problematic, since it overlooks scenarios in which emotional fluctuations arise from heightened positive affect rather than distress. This issue has been widely discussed in neuroticism research, in which cultural biases often equate emotional variability with psychological dysfunction, despite evidence that emotional shifts can sometimes reflect adaptive flexibility (Daniel et al., 2024). Future iterations of the MPI may benefit from reframing this item to clarify whether it reflects emotional dysregulation or general affective variability.

Moreover, the compassion item may have response-process validity issues, since its pictographic representation includes a heart: a symbol commonly associated with love and affection in a broad, Westernized sense rather than the Buddhist conceptualization of compassion, which emphasizes the recognition and alleviation of suffering. This potential misinterpretation could explain why the compassion item did not distinguish LKM from other groups, as participants may have associated the heart icon with general warmth, kindness or positive affect rather than with compassion as a distinct construct (Gilbert et al., 2019; Kirby et al., 2022). Experts in Phase 1 had already noted this ambiguity, as well as the visual overlap between the heart symbols of the compassion, self-compassion, and warmth items (Supplementary Materials, Table S1.2). In addition, self-reports of compassion (with more precise contents regarding suffering) did not show improvements beyond controls. Refining the visual representation of compassion in the MPI (e.g., by incorporating imagery that more explicitly conveys compassion conceptualization) could improve the scale's ability to distinguish compassionate states from generalized positive affect.

Reliability

Regarding reliability, the MPI seems to follow a gradient from the positive cluster (adequate on every index) through the negative (adequate for relative but weaker for absolute decisions) to the heterogeneous cluster (preliminary and unreliable in most). Within this gradient, three item profiles stand out. Reference Continuum, Warmth, and Positive Affect show fair temporal stability, the highest criterion-based floors, and robust ρ(.40) values. In contrast, Time Fast and Time Disappearing were weak on all indices, suggesting genuinely noisy single-item measurement of time-distortion at rest. Finally and surprisingly, Hyper-ego was the most temporally stable item of the inventory (ICC = .73), yet showed almost null criterion-based reliability. That is, the item seems to measure something highly consistent that is simply unrelated to the available criteria. This gives relevance to assessing multiple complementary sources of reliability evidence for single-item instruments. The large MDCs, finally, indicate that individual-level change on single MPI items should be interpreted with caution, and that detecting individual change reliably would require aggregation across items, as the cluster-level G-coefficients suggest. Thus, triangulation of multi-source reliability evidence has provided coherent results, with the positive cluster adequate on every index, the negative cluster adequate for relative but weaker for absolute decisions (Φ = .49), and the heterogeneous cluster exploratory throughout. Crucially, the sources also showed informative mixed patterns.

Strengths and Limitations

This study has several strengths. First, it extends pictographic assessment, previously limited to single dimensions such as body boundaries or spatial frame of reference (Dambrun, 2016; Hanley & Garland, 2019), to a broad set of meditation-related experiences. Second, it combines multiple sources of validity and reliability evidence within a coordinated framework, integrating phenomenological interviews and quantitative analyses. Third, it uses a randomized design with an active control, preregistration, sensitivity analyses reporting the minimum detectable effects for all tests, and openly available data, code, and materials. Taken together, the study provides initial evidence for the MPI and a framework for evaluating batteries of single-item measures more broadly. However, several limitations are present.

The study did not include follow-up measurements, which impedes exploring dynamics of the MPI. An intensive longitudinal design such as ecological momentary assessment of meditation related states (e.g., Bai et al., 2020; Parola et al., preprint); would provide richer insights. Future studies could adopt methodologies such as multilevel vector autoregressive networks combined with intensive longitudinal data to provide a more granular understanding of temporal dynamics. In addition, meditations were limited to single-session practices, not representative of sustained meditative practice. Future research should investigate changes in the MPI across manualized interventions, such as Mindfulness or Compassion-Based Interventions, to better understand its effects. This could be complemented by an examination of profiles of responses to meditation experiences, both as punctual experiences and as a form of training.

Regarding measurement, the study relied exclusively on self-report measures, which may introduce biases such as social desirability or limited introspective accuracy. Future studies should adopt a multimodal approach to examine how behavioral data, neural measures (e.g., fMRI or EEG), and other-reported assessments correlate with self-reported MPI scores, in line with neurophenomenological approaches to meditation (Lutz et al., 2024). This would provide a more comprehensive understanding of the construct.

Regarding item development, each pictographic item was accompanied by a brief verbal definition, and the question named the target construct. Thus, present data cannot fully erase the verbal-translation bias, although provide some control on it. Future studies could test MPI items with and without definitions and labels. In addition, beyond a preliminary comprehensibility check with researchers without meditation experience, no formal interpretability study (e.g., cognitive interviews) was conducted with lay participants. This may imply that non-meditators may interpret some items differently from experienced practitioners, potentially affecting validity across groups, a concern already identified for other meditation-related assessment tools (e.g., Belzer et al., 2013). Future research should explicitly test measurement invariance, scale's validity and sensitivity and examine whether the MPI functions equivalently in meditators and non-meditators as well as those with advanced meditation experience vs those receiving manualized interventions, since their psychological states may exhibit distinct patterns compared to those of novice or lay practitioners. Finally, the MPI does not currently include items for meta-awareness or equanimity (due to the difficulty in representing them pictographically), which have been proposed as key mechanisms of mindfulness-induced change (Cásedas et al., 2024).

Regarding the sample, its size fell short of the a priori power analysis target. Future research should prioritize recruiting large, high-powered samples to ensure generalizability. Moreover, the sample was drawn from Spain and Spanish-speaking countries, was mostly female (80.5%) and students (55.7%), and came from WEIRD contexts with a predominantly Christian cultural background. The findings may not fully generalize to populations with different cultural or religious contexts. Cross-cultural comparisons seem to hold potential, such as countries with a Buddhist tradition, or among other relevant groups, such as clinical populations.

Regarding item clusters, some response bias (e.g., social desirability) or third variables could be explaining these groupings. Relatedly, discriminant validity was not formally tested: many items correlated with most self-reports in the same direction, which may partly reflect a general affective valence underlying the positive and negative clusters. Future studies should test whether each item correlates more strongly with its matched construct than with unrelated ones, and whether potential biases or dispositions could impact the grouping. In addition, some correlations between items and self-reports were underpowered, raising caution in interpretation. Manipulation checks remained in only some variables, and incremental prediction did not remain after the inclusion of baseline scores in any cases. The items may therefore be exposed to uncontrolled error sources, and may predict future levels through their relations with other variables rather than predicting change over and above baseline stability.

Reliability analysis holds several limitations since temporal stability would be enriched with more time measurements. In addition, the attenuation-formula simulation relies on classical test theory and thus should be held as exploratory. Results of analyses that deviated from the preregistration (Supplementary Materials, Section S2.0) should be considered exploratory. In summary, while this study offers a foundation for understanding the MPI, addressing these limitations in future research will strengthen the validity and applicability of the findings. By using intensive longitudinal designs, larger and more diverse samples, structured interventions, multimodal measurements, and expert populations, future studies can enhance the field's understanding of this multidimensional construct.

Beyond the MPI itself, a main contribution of this work is the coordinated multi-source framework through which it was validated. The value of the framework lies in how sources of evidence are organized in a mutually constraining argument, which allowed inferences that no source could license alone. Response-process evidence from Phase 1 anticipated anomalies (e.g., the ambiguity of the compassion icon) that would otherwise have been difficult to interpret. Reliability and criterion evidence revealed that an item can be highly stable yet unrelated to its criteria, a dissociation that would be masked when items are aggregated into multi-item scores. Sensitivity-to-change evidence showed that mean-level change occurred without reorganization of the measurement structure. As a checklist, these analyses would document that the MPI "passed" several criteria; but as a coordinated framework, they yield a calibrated account of what each item seems to measure, and subsequent trust on its uses. We propose this validation framework as applicable to the growing class of single-item measures beyond classical frameworks.

Conclusion

This study addresses a persistent methodological challenge in meditation research, namely the reliance on verbal self-report for phenomena that are embodied, transient and often ineffable, by developing and validating the Meditation Pictographic Inventory, based on a multi-source framework. A subset of its items appears sensitive to meditation-induced change; items relate to other constructs in the expected direction, predict future levels (but not change) of relevant outcomes, and are organized in three clusters of experiences, with no detectable structural change from pre to post despite mean-level changes. Our approach aimed to bridge the limitations of both quantitative and phenomenological methods and to offer a tool capable of capturing a broader spectrum of meditation-related experiential dimensions. Beyond the instrument itself, the multi-source validation framework applied here offers a template for validating multi-single-item inventories more broadly, an increasingly common format in experience sampling and state assessment. By visually representing complex phenomena, the MPI offers a complementary, broad-coverage measurement option while preserving the phenomenological richness of meditative experiences. This integration of quantitative and qualitative methodologies highlights the potential of pictographic tools to offer a more comprehensive and multidimensional understanding of meditation practices, self-related processes and altered states of consciousness.

Phase 1 -Development

Phase 1 -Development • Absorption is the capacity for deep immersion in sensory or imaginative experiences, leading to a temporary restructuring of self-boundaries and reduced awareness of the surroundings (Tellegen & Atkinson, 1974).

S1.1 Definitions of the concepts

• Affect refers to the immediate emotional experience reflecting an individual's activation and engagement with their environment (Roca et al., 2023). Positive affect involves high energy, alertness, and pleasurable engagement, whereas negative affect reflects distress and unpleasurable emotions such as anger, fear, and guilt.

• Body awareness refers to the conscious recognition and perception of one's own body, including its movements, sensations, and position in space (Mehling et al., 2012).

• Body boundaries refer to the degree to which the self is experienced as a discrete, body-encapsulated entity, perceived as separate and isolated from the surrounding world (Dambrun, 2016).

• Compassion refers to the feeling of being emotionally moved by others' suffering, accompanied by the motivation to alleviate their distress (Goetz et al., 2010).

• Connectedness with others or nature refers to the perceived overlap between the self and others (Aron et al., 1992) or the natural world (Schultz, 2001), reflecting a sense of closeness and unity in one's social and environmental relationships.

• Decentering refers to the ability to step outside of one's immediate thoughts and emotions, observing them with perspective and reducing their impact on self-identification, thereby altering the nature of the experience (Bernstein et al., 2015).

• Distortion of time: Faster or slower refers to the subjective awareness of time's passage, which may appear to speed up or slow down depending on cognitive and emotional states (Droit-Volet et al., 2017).

• Emotional Reactivity refers to the tendency to respond to internal experiences (thoughts, emotions, bodily sensations) with intensity and persistence, often becoming attached to them, rather than observing them with detachment and equanimity (Baer et al., 2006).

• Emotional stability refers to the ability to maintain a balanced emotional state, responding to positive and negative experiences with resilience and minimal emotional fluctuations (Costa & McCrae, 1992). In the final version, this item was reverse-coded and renamed emotional instability (see main text).

• Ineffability refers to the experience of being unable or unwilling to put one's current state or sensations into words, often due to their profound, abstract, or transcendent nature (Dambrun, 2016).

• Mental effort refers to the subjective experience of how easy or difficult it is to sustain cognitive engagement in a given task, reflecting the allocation of attentional and cognitive resources (Kahneman, 1973).

• Mind-wandering refers to the decoupling of attention from an ongoing task, shifting focus to self-generated thoughts and feelings unrelated to the present activity or environment (Smallwood & Schooler, 2006).

• Reference continuum refers to the experience of self, in which the boundaries of the self become more relaxed, allowing the spatial frame of reference to extend beyond the physical body (Hanley & Garland, 2019).

• Self-compassion refers to the ability to be open to one's own suffering without avoidance or disconnection, instead responding with kindness and a desire to alleviate distress and promote healing (Neff, 2003).

• Self-criticism refers to the tendency to evaluate oneself negatively, often harshly, in response to a perceived failure or mistake, which can impact emotional well-being and self-worth (Gilbert et al., 2004).

• Sense of Self: Hypo-ego refers to a diminished sense of self-focus, where individuals experience a reduced sense of self-boundaries, decreased self-referential processing, and a greater sense of interconnectedness with others or the environment (Leary & Guadagno, 2011); Hyper-ego refers to an exaggerated sense of self-focus, characterized by heightened self-referential thinking, self-consciousness, and an increased perception of separation from others and the environment (Leary, 2004).

• Time Disappearing refers to the experience of a complete lack of temporal orientation, where individuals lose the sense of past, present, and future, often associated with altered states of consciousness (Metzinger, 2024, Ch. 22).

• Warmth refers to a warm sensation in the center of the chest, often accompanied by a distinct feeling in this area, typically associated with positive emotional experiences (Lutz et al., 2008).

Model fit was assessed with the Comparative Fit Index (CFI), the Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI), the Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA), and the Standardized Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR). Criteria for acceptable fit were values > .90 for CFI and TLI, and < .08 for RMSEA and SRMR. Raw mean scores were computed and compared with factor scores to ensure comparability of the instrument's properties. Fit indices for each self-report are available in the Zenodo repository..

S2.2 Power and replicability of psychometric networks

To estimate the network's stability, we performed power and replicability analyses of random networks via simulations. More concretely, we simulated networks with three clusters (two moderately connected and one weakly connected) and ordinal nodes with [7] values, estimated with EBICglasso. Note that the empirical network was estimated with ggmModSelect. The difference between power and replicability simulations is that power simulations estimate the performance of an estimation method relative to the true model and across various sample sizes. In contrast, replicability simulations estimate how well a network based on a second, independent sample would replicate a first network. Results are displayed in Figures S1 and S2. For our sample size (N = 378), simulations indicated 80% sensitivity, 99% specificity, 80% replicated non-zero edges, and 95% replicated zero edges.

S2.6 Effects of meditation experience

Meditation experience showed a significant effect on the following items: Compassion (η²p = .010*!), Decentering (η²p = .030** ! ), Positive Affect (η²p = .020** ! ), Self-Compassion (η²p = .010* ! ), Connectedness with Nature (η²p = .030** ! ), Warmth (η²p = .030*** ! ), Emotional Instability (η²p = .110***), Ineffability (η²p = .040*** ! ), Mental Effort (η²p = .050*** ! ), Mind-Wandering (η²p = .060*** ! ), Negative Affect (η²p = .090***), Emotional Reactivity (η²p = .320***), Self-Criticism (η²p = .070***). However, most of these effects were below the minimum detectable effect size (η²p = .063), except for (sorted by effect size) Emotional Reactivity, emotional instability, Negative Affect, and self-criticism. Estimated marginal means with 95%CIs were screened for those items (Figure S5).

For these four items, patterns were similar across time and groups in both meditators and non-meditators. That is, scores on these items decreased in all or most groups, including the control group. The only exception was Emotional Reactivity, which showed a clear and significant descent in non-meditators but non-significant patterns in meditators, although descriptively there are also descents. Overall, meditation experience was associated with detectable differences in level, but of limited relevance for change, since patterns of change were mostly similar across experience levels.

S2.7 Incremental prediction (regressions)

On the covariate selection, the hierarchical regression models including MPI items as predictors were added. While the general analytic plan was preregistered, specific covariate blocks were constructed post hoc based on: (1) Theoretical correspondence between MPI item domains and established self-report measures (see Table S5 for item-level mappings); (2) Established nomological networks from prior meditation research (e.g., mindfulness correlates with decentering, compassion correlates with self-compassion and positive affect); (3) Minimizing multicollinearity (VIF < 5 for all covariate sets).

We documented all covariate selections before model estimation, and the full specification is available in the Zenodo repository. We acknowledge this is an exploratory analytic decision; therefore, interpret significance tests as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.

Assumption checks for MRAs Assumption Criterion S-DERS HAAS-pos Linearity Scatterplots and RESET with p < .05 59% pass (acceptable*) 71% pass (acceptable*) No influential cases Cook's distance > 1 100% pass 100% pass No collinearity VIF > 10 100% pass 100% pass Normality of residuals Shapiro-Wilk with p < .05 and |skewness| > 2 or |kurtosis| > 7; QQ plot 100% uncertain (acceptable*) 47% pass (acceptable*) Homoskedasticit y of residuals Breusch-Pagan with p < .05; Scatterplot of residuals vs predicted 80% pass (acceptable*) 46% pass (acceptable*) Independence of residuals Durbin-Watson with p < .05 100% pass* 91% pass* Note. *Acceptable is due to estimating with bootstrap, big sample (n = 378) and lack of influential cases combined with almost all with independent residuals. In the case of independence of residuals, 39% and 67% pass with sorted data by group but when scrambled they rise to 90-100%. For every step-2 model, we examined independence (Durbin-Watson), multicollinearity (VIF/tolerance), influential cases (Cook's distance), normality of residuals (Q-Q plots, skewness and kurtosis), homoscedasticity (studentized Breusch-Pagan), and linearity (RESET). Multicollinearity (100% of models within criteria; all VIF < 10) and influential cases (no Cook's D > 1 in any model) were unproblematic (Table S7).

Residual normality was acceptable in all models by distributional shape (all |skewness| ≤ 2 and excess kurtosis ≤ 7), although Shapiro-Wilk tests were significant in 70% of models, as expected at this sample size. Breusch-Pagan and RESET tests were significant in 41% and 39% of models, respectively; note that inference did not rely on homoscedasticity or exact functional form, as significance decisions used BH-corrected tests and precision was quantified with stratified case bootstrapping, which is robust to both. The full assumption table (one row per model) is available in the Zenodo repository. DW tests were significant in a majority of models (57-70% depending on outcome and test laterality). A row-permutation diagnostic showed that this reflects the data-collection order rather than model misspecification: refitting every model with randomly permuted rows reduced significant DW tests to the nominal rate (0-9%), and residuals showed no linear trend across file order, indicating local segment structure consistent with group-session data collection. As no session identifier was recorded, session-level clustering could not be modeled directly and is acknowledged as a limitation; the intervention arm -the main clustering sourcewas included in all models. Finally, adding the pre-score of each dependent variable to the covariate block nullified all incremental effects: across the 46 models, all ΔR² ≤ .005 and all BH-corrected p ≥ .05, with no item significant for either outcome (Table S6). Together with the main results, this indicates that MPI items forecast future levels of dysregulation and positive affect largely through their association with concurrent baseline standing, and do not predict change beyond baseline stability over this short pre-post window. Full sensitivity coefficients are available in the Zenodo repository.

Figure S6.

Scatterplot of standardized slopes of MRAs indicating mirror effects by cluster.

It can be observed in Figure S6 that a mirror effect is present regarding predictive capability of MPI items. More concretely, items in the positive cluster show negative slopes when predicting emotional dysregulation (S-DERS) while positive slopes when predicting positive affect (HAAS-pos).

Figure S7 Bland-Altman plots for each item Attenuation-based sensitivity curves. Figure S8 shows the item-level curves (pre and post overlaid) and Figure S9 shows the pooled pre and post curves. The x-axis is reversed so that the most conservative assumption (ρ = 1) appears leftmost; estimates rise as the assumed true correlation relaxes toward its empirical lower bound. Dotted horizontal lines mark the .40 (fair) benchmark for lower-bound reliability of the MPI items was .06 at pre-intervention and .07 at post-intervention, rising steeply as the assumed true correlation approached its empirical lower bound (e.g., .24 and .28, respectively, at ρ_ic = .50). Item-level curves fell into three patterns. Items of the positive cluster showed the strongest criterion-based reliability: their estimates remained clearly above zero across the entire imputation range, with conservative floors between .01 and .21 (e.g., Warmth = .21, PosEmo = .17). Items of the negative cluster showed intermediate values (floors of .02-.13), with a consistent post-intervention attenuation (e.g., NegEmo declining from .09 to .04) attributable to the general pre-to-post reduction in negative-cluster scores, which compresses their variance. Finally, for the heterogeneous-cluster items (e.g., HyperEgo, TimeSlow), the observed item-criterion correlations were too weak (≤ .11) for the method to be informative: their curves collapse toward zero under nearly all assumptions, which reflects the absence of nomological ties to the present criteria rather Pooled item-criterion sensitivity curves at pre and post. S2.4 Manipulation check: effects of the three meditation practices on state self-reports

To further investigate the effects of different meditation practices (CBM, LKM, DIM) on psychological states, we conducted 4 (Group) × 2 (Time) ANOVAs and analyzed estimated marginal means and confidence intervals for each group and time point (pre and post) of the state self-report measures (see Figure S3). The results were interpreted based on the confidence intervals (CIs) shown in the figure, with non-overlapping CIs indicating statistically significant differences between groups and time points.

S2.5 Effects of the three meditation practices on MPI items over time

To assess the effects of the three meditation practices on the MPI items over time, we conducted a series of 4×2 ANCOVAs (Time × Group), reporting F-statistics and effect sizes (Table S4). Estimated marginal means and 95% CIs of the MPI items by group and time are shown in Figure S4.

Main effects of group results. Results in Table S4. Significant group differences emerged for body awareness, F(3, 373) = 4.75, p < .01, η²p = .04; body boundaries, F = 2.75, p < .05, η²p = .02; compassion, F = 3.27, p < .05, η²p = .03; positive affect, F = 6.22, p < .001, η²p = .05; reference continuum, F = 4.21, p < .01, η²p = .03; self-compassion, F = 5.09, p < .01, η²p = .04; connectedness with others, F = 2.63, p < .05, η²p = .02; warmth, F = 10.50, p < .001, η²p = .08; time disappearing, F = 3.94, p < .01, η²p = .03; and time slow, F = 2.75, p < .05, η²p = .02. Because groups were randomized, these main effects average over pre and post and should be interpreted through the Group × Time interactions below.

Main effects of time. Scores changed from pre to post on 19 of the 23 items (all except connectedness with nature, ineffability, mental effort, and hypo-ego). The largest effects were decreases in emotional Emotional Reactivity, F(1, 373) = 235.52, p < .001, η²p = .39; negative affect, F = 155.56, p < .001, η²p = .29; self-criticism, F = 139.10, p < .001, η²p = .27; and emotional instability, F = 64.60, p < .001, η²p = .15, together with an increase in reference continuum, F = 54.00, p < .001, η²p = .13. Group × Time interactions. Significant interactions emerged for nine items: body awareness, F(3, 373) = 12.40, p < .001, η²p = .09; self-compassion, F = 10.80, p < .001, η²p = .08; body boundaries, F = 7.64, p < .001, η²p = .06; reference continuum, F = 6.58, p < .001, η²p = .05; warmth, F = 6.52, p < .001, η²p = .05; time disappearing, F = 5.55, p < .001, η²p = .04; mind wandering, F = 4.59, p < .01, η²p = .04; positive affect, F = 3.71, p < .05, η²p = .03; and mental effort, F = 3.57, p < .05, η²p = .03. At the cluster level, the interaction was significant for the positive cluster score, F = 11.71, p < .001, η²p = .09, but not for the negative or heterogeneous scores.

Post hoc comparisons for the significant interactions are reported in the main text.

S2.8 Reliability analysis and plots

Bland-Altman analyses (control group, n = 92). Limits of agreement equal twice the MDC₉₅ by construction, providing the visual counterpart of Table 2 in the Main Text. The plots (Figure S7) revealed a systematic downward drift for 12 of 23 items -most pronounced in the negative cluster (e.g., Self-Criticism, bias = -1.37; Emotional Reactivity, -1.15; Negative Affect, -1.14) -consistent with a session effect (regression to the mean, familiarization) rather than measurement error; for this reason the consistency coefficient ICC(3,1), insensitive to uniform level shifts, was preferred over absolute-agreement alternatives. Proportional bias was detected for five items, most clearly Time Fast (slope = -.50, p = .003; larger decreases among high scorers, a regression-to-the-mean signature) and Hypo-Ego (slope = +.37, p = .005; larger discrepancies at higher score levels).

ICC-type coefficients (Cicchetti, 1994). Because the averaged criterion reliability is very consistent (α ≈ .86), each curve is fully characterized by the two indices reported in Table 2 in the Main Text (floor and ρ(.40). Internal structure-based validity: Psychometric Networks of the MPIFollowing the order of validity sources proposed by the Standards (AERA, APA, & NCME, 2014), internal-structure evidence is reported first, as the clusters identified in the network analysis are subsequently used to organize, but not to replace, item-level results.At baseline, Exploratory Graph Analysis (EGA, Figure1) with the walktrap and Louvain algorithms yielded the same three clusters of items: (i) positive experiences (absorption, body awareness, body boundaries, compassion, decentering, positive affect, reference continuum, self-compassion, connectedness with nature, connectedness with others, and warmth); (ii) negative experiences (emotional instability, ineffability, mental effort, mind wandering, negative affect, emotional Emotional Reactivity, and self-criticism); and (iii) a heterogeneous cluster of weakly inter-correlated items concerning distortions in time perception and sense of self (time fast, time slow, time disappearing, hypo-ego, and hyper-ego). Consistent with the item-level approach, these clusters are interpreted as descriptive groupings of related experiences rather than latent constructs.
